source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Soar RL puts Q values in numeric preference rules. RL only breaks ties when other preferences are not enough, so hand-written knowledge guards against danger and RL tunes the rest.
numbers: Supports Q-learning, SARSA, eligibility traces. Learning and discount rates fixed at agent start. No intrinsic reward built in (appraisal reward only in an experimental version).
quote: RL influences operator selection only when the other, non-RL preferences are insufficient for making a decision.
limits: Review by the architecture's author, not an independent test. No effect sizes given.
agent_relevance: Matches G5 and the S6 idea: learned scores only decide when rule-based preferences are silent. Keep learned operator preference as a tie-breaker, never a veto.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Soar RL applies in every substate with independent rewards, so planning in a substate gives model-based RL and the top state gives model-free RL. RL rules can also be created by chunking and then tuned by reward.
numbers: Value function is many relational rules; tile coding and coarse coding are cited as speed-ups (Wang and Laird 2007).
limits: Claim of speed-up is cited from other papers; numbers not restated here.
agent_relevance: Supports a per-class record in S0: value estimates for operators kept per problem class and updated from real outcome, not model opinion (G2).

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Semantic memory is a graph store with cue-based retrieval. Best match uses base-level activation (recency, frequency, noise) plus spreading activation from working memory. Soar has no automatic learning into semantic memory; the agent must store deliberately.
numbers: Reason given for a separate store: cost of rule matching grows significantly with working memory size.
quote: Soar does not have an automatic learning mechanism for semantic memory, but an agent can deliberately store information at any time.
limits: No retrieval accuracy numbers in this text. Human-fit claim cited to Schatz et al. 2018.
agent_relevance: Our S0 class record should be written by an explicit code step, not automatically by the model. Keep the working context small and fetch records by cue.

source: Laird (2022) Introduction to the Soar Cognitive Architecture
finding: Episodic memory stores a snapshot of the top state after every decision. Retrieval is by partial-state cue, biased to recency. Cost to fetch old episodes rises slowly with store size; recent ones stay constant. Author lists uses: virtual sensing, action models, retrospective operator evaluation, prospective memory.
numbers: Episodic memory has no generalisation mechanism (author states this).
quote: Episodic learning has often been ignored as a learning method because it does not have generalization mechanisms.
limits: Uses are cited, not measured here.
agent_relevance: Raw episode logs help but do not generalise alone. An LLM agent needs a separate step that distils episodes into class-level rules.

source: Derbinsky, Li, Laird (2012) Algorithms for Scaling in a General Episodic Memory (AAMAS extended abstract)
finding: Soar episodic memory scaled to hours or days of real time. A modified cue-matching algorithm grew search time 3.6x slower before the exploration-to-patrol shift and 4.9x slower after, versus baseline.
numbers: Over 100 cues, 44 instances of 12 planning domains, 3 video games, robotics. Robot task 12 h: baseline stored over 58M episodes, variant nearly 109M. Baseline max cue-match exceeded 50 ms in under 12 h. Variant projected reactive to about 694M episodes (>3 days).
quote: Our variant algorithm can continue to provide reactive real-time cue-matching performance for nearly 694M episodes.
limits: Extended abstract; one cue (goal management) shown in detail. Authors say it did not greatly impact performance in most tasks. Projection is extrapolated. Xeon 2.26 GHz, Soar 9.3.1.
agent_relevance: Retrieval cost grows with store size even in a purpose-built system. An LLM agent should cap the S0 record store and index by class, not scan a growing log.

source: Derbinsky, Li, Laird (2012) Algorithms for Scaling in a General Episodic Memory
finding: Boundary condition: scaling depends on cue type and on whether distinct structures grow over the agent's life. The robot goal cue got slower as the target goal got further back in time.
numbers: Both algorithms showed growing cue-match time on the goal-management cue; growth rate slowed after the agent finished exploring (about 8M baseline, 12M variant episodes).
limits: Gain shown mainly in one task class; simple cues may lose from extra upkeep cost (authors say so).
agent_relevance: Old records are costly to find. Prefer recency-weighted retrieval for class records.

source: Wallace, Dickinson, Nuxoll (2013) Hashing for Lightweight Episodic Recall (AAAI Spring Symposium)
finding: Plain Soar RL fails when state is hidden. A side module (ZigguSoar) tracks reward variance per operator rule and, when variance shows hidden state, specialises rules on one-step history. This fixes learning without full episodic retrieval.
numbers: Flip environment, first 10,000 steps, 20 runs, 100-step moving average. Baseline Soar learned only the deterministic Up prediction; ZigguSoar learned predictions for both Up and Left. Rule count grows without bound as needed history lengthens.
quote: If the confidence intervals are significantly different based on the incoming action, this suggests that the agent would benefit from refining its notion of s.
limits: Toy environments (Flip, Well World). No hard percentage in the text; results are in figures. Authors call their methods early predecessors of the state of the art.
agent_relevance: Direct analogue: if a score for an operator has high variance, the class record is too coarse and should be split. Use variance as the code-checked signal to refine class definitions (G1: act on a signal).

source: Wallace, Dickinson, Nuxoll (2013) Hashing for Lightweight Episodic Recall
finding: Cost argument: avoid full episodic recall because retrieval cost rises with lifespan; a hash of recent history gives constant cost.
numbers: Authors claim performance scales regardless of agent lifespan; supported only by the rule-count and step curves.
limits: Small experiment, single research group.
agent_relevance: Keep memory reads constant-cost: fetch by hash of class, not by search over history.

source: Pink et al. (2025) Position: Episodic Memory is the Missing Piece for Long-Term LLM Agents
finding: Position paper names five properties of episodic memory for LLM agents and a roadmap; it argues for consolidation from an external store into parameters. It reports no new experiment.
numbers: No measured results. Linux example (40M lines) used as motivation. Asks for constant cost per new token and stable or improving performance.
limits: Position paper: argument, not evidence. Consolidation into weights is out of scope for a no-training scaffold.
agent_relevance: Treat as a design checklist, not evidence. Our scaffold does the external store plus retrieval into context part only.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)
finding: Maps Soar-style memories onto LLM agents: working, episodic, semantic, procedural. Reflexion and Generative Agents write LLM inferences from episodes into semantic memory. Retrieval-augmented NLP is read as retrieval from a semantic store.
numbers: Conceptual framework; no benchmark numbers.
quote: Reflexion uses an LLM to reflect on failed episodes and stores the results as semantic knowledge.
limits: Mapping is by analogy.
agent_relevance: Confirms our split: raw episodes (S0 log) versus distilled knowledge (class record). Write distillation as a separate code-triggered step.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Verbal reflection stored in an episodic buffer works as RL without weight updates. ReAct plus Reflexion solved 130 of 134 ALFWorld tasks over 12 trials; ReAct-only stalled between trials 6 and 7.
numbers: ALFWorld absolute gain 22% over strong baselines in 12 steps; HotPotQA +20%; HumanEval pass@1 91.0 vs GPT-4 80.1. ReAct-only hallucination rate stayed at 22%.
quote: ReAct + Reflexion significantly outperforms ReAct by completing 130 out of 134 tasks
limits: Memory limit of 1 to 3 experiences. MBPP Python Reflexion 77.1 was below GPT-4 baseline 80.1. WebShop gave no gain (needs diverse behavior).
agent_relevance: Verbal feedback memory works when the environment gives a real signal. Ties to G2.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Ablation on the 50 hardest HumanEval Rust problems: removing self-generated tests dropped accuracy to 52% vs 60% baseline; removing the written reflection gave no gain over baseline (60%); full Reflexion 68%.
numbers: Table 3: omit tests 52%; omit self-reflection 60%; full 68%. N = 50 problems. False positive test rate 16.3% on MBPP Python vs 1.4% on HumanEval Python.
quote: The agent is unable to determine if the current implementation is correct without unit tests.
limits: Small N (50). Reflection helps only when a real test signal exists; without tests the agent cannot tell if code is right and makes harmful edits.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G2/G3: memory learning needs an external check. Reflection without a real signal is neutral or harmful.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
finding: Memory stream with recency, importance and relevance retrieval, plus reflection. Ablating memory, planning and reflection lowered rated believability step by step.
numbers: 100 Prolific raters ranked 5 conditions. TrueSkill mean: full 29.89, no reflection 26.88, no reflection or planning 25.64, human crowdworkers 22.95, no memory/planning/reflection 21.21. Full vs fully ablated Cohen's d = 8.16. Kruskal-Wallis chi2(4)=150.29, p<0.001.
quote: The full architecture produced the most believable behavior; performance degraded with removal of each component.
limits: Outcome is believability rated by humans, not task correctness. Authors report agents embellish memories. Single simulation.
agent_relevance: Evidence that retrieval plus reflection beat no memory, but only on a believability metric. Does not show a task accuracy gain.

source: Wu et al. (2025) LongMemEval: Benchmarking Chat Assistants on Long-Term Interactive Memory (ICLR 2025)
finding: Memory-augmented commercial assistants lose much accuracy versus reading the evidence directly. Long-context LLMs drop 30 to 60% on the long version.
numbers: 500 questions, 5 abilities. ChatGPT (GPT-4o) 0.5773 and Coze (GPT-4o) 0.3299 vs offline reading GPT-4o 0.9184 (drops 37% and 64%). GPT-4o oracle 0.870 vs 0.606 on long version (30.3% drop); Llama 3.1 8B 0.660 vs 0.342 (48.1% drop).
limits: Evaluator agrees >97% with human experts. Tested on chat history, not agent tasks.
agent_relevance: Memory read is the bottleneck: storing history is not the same as using it. Test any S0 retrieval against a no-memory arm and an oracle-evidence arm.

source: Wu et al. (2025) LongMemEval
finding: Index and query design moves recall: expanding keys with extracted user facts and time-aware query filtering both help.
numbers: Fact-augmented key expansion: +9.4% recall@k and +5.4% accuracy on average. Time-aware query expansion: +11.3% recall with rounds, +6.8% with sessions. Correct retrieval but wrong generation is 15-19% of all instances (40-50% of errors).
limits: Time gain needs a strong LLM for time-range extraction; Llama 8B gave less. Condensed keys alone (summary, keyphrase) did not beat raw text.
agent_relevance: Store class records with facts plus raw text as key; filter by time. Expect many errors to come from reading, not retrieval.

source: Maharana et al. (2024) Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents (LoCoMo)
finding: Long-context and RAG help but stay far below humans, mostly on temporal reasoning. Long-context models are easily misled by adversarial questions.
numbers: Conversations about 300 turns, 9K tokens, up to 35 sessions. Human overall F1 87.9. Best model overall 32.4 (gpt-4-turbo). Gaps: 56% overall, 73% temporal. gpt-3.5-turbo-16K adversarial F1 2.1 vs 22.1 (Llama-2-Chat) and 70.2 (GPT-4-turbo, 4K). RAG on stored observations gave about 5% gain over raw dialog.
limits: Older models (2023). Dialogues machine-generated then human-edited (about 15% turns edited). F1 partial-match metric is crude.
agent_relevance: Time reasoning is the weak spot of memory reads. Store dates as fields and compare in code (G5).

source: MemGPT (Packer et al. 2023) MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
finding: Self-managed paged memory (main context plus archival store) lifts deep memory retrieval and multi-hop lookup.
numbers: Deep memory retrieval accuracy: GPT-3.5 38.7% to 66.9%; GPT-4 32.1% to 92.5%; GPT-4 Turbo 35.3% to 93.4% with MemGPT. Nested key-value retrieval: GPT-4 baseline reaches 0% by 3 nesting levels; MemGPT with GPT-4 unaffected by nesting.
limits: Needs strong function calling: GPT-3.5 MemGPT degraded on document QA and dropped at 2 nesting levels. Synthetic or persona-based tasks.
agent_relevance: Model-driven memory paging works only with a strong model. In our scaffold the program should decide reads and writes (section 1).

source: Chhikara et al. (2025) Mem0: Building Production-Ready AI Agents with Scalable Long-Term Memory
finding: Vendor paper: extracted-memory store is close to full context at much lower cost, but full context scored higher.
numbers: LoCoMo LLM-as-judge: full-context 72.90, Mem0g 68.44, Mem0 66.88, Zep 65.99, LangMem 58.10, OpenAI memory 52.90, A-Mem 48.38. Claims 26% relative gain over OpenAI, 91% lower p95 latency, over 90% token saving (full-context p95 17.1 s vs Mem0 1.44 s).
limits: Authors' own system and own re-runs of baselines. Graph variant strong on temporal, not on multi-hop.
agent_relevance: Memory buys cost, not accuracy, when the whole history fits. Do not expect S0 records to beat full context at small scale.

source: Hu, Wang, McAuley (2026) Evaluating Memory in LLM Agents via Incremental Multi-Turn Interactions (MemoryAgentBench, ICLR 2026)
finding: Independent test: structured memory agents often do worse than their plain backbone. RAG wins retrieval, long context wins test-time learning and long-range understanding, and all methods fail at selective forgetting.
numbers: Overall: GPT-4o-mini 42.3; BM25 RAG 41.5; HippoRAG-v2 41.6; Mem0 21.1; Cognee 20.6; Zep 24.0; GPT-5-mini long context 60.6. Multi-hop fact update: all methods at most 28%. o4-mini FactCon-MH 80.0 at 6K but 14.0 at 32K.
quote: all methods fail on the multi-hop situation (with achieving at most 28% accuracy)
limits: Mem0 here scores far below Mem0's own paper; benchmarks and configs differ, so this is a replication-style gap. Single paper.
agent_relevance: Overwriting stale class records is the hard part. Version records and resolve conflicts in code, not by the model.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: An Empirical Study of Experience-Following Behavior
finding: Agents copy retrieved experience: output similarity rises with input similarity. So wrong stored records spread (error propagation) and correct but ill-fitting ones mislead (misaligned replay).
numbers: Four agents (including RegAgent, AgentDriver, EhrAgent) with add-all, coarse and strict selective addition. Strict selective addition on AgentDriver lagged at first, then passed the error-free ground-truth variant after about 2000 executions; add-all and coarse selection widened the gap.
quote: LLM agents display an experience-following property: high similarity between a task input and the input in a retrieved memory record often results in highly similar agent outputs.
limits: Exact percentage gains not captured; effects read from figures. Short, task-specific agents.
agent_relevance: Add to memory only when a strict external check passes. Delete by later utility. Later task outcomes act as free quality labels. Fits G2, G3 and the S9 gating idea.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents
finding: History-based deletion removes records whose later retrieval led to low utility. It improved long-term performance in the agents tested and under task-distribution shift.
numbers: Compared add-only and deletion variants (periodic, history-based) across the agents; exact deltas not captured.
limits: Needs a utility evaluator; a noisy evaluator removes good records. One agent saw a smaller gain.
agent_relevance: Prune class records by downstream result with a code-run evaluator.

source: Fan, Lan (2026) From Cognitive Architectures to Language Agents: A Mechanism-Level Review
finding: Review of 10 architectures and 42 modern systems. Modern agents rebuilt adaptive memory and failure recovery by independent convergence, not documented inheritance from Soar. Soar chunking is mapped to AgentHER and Reflexion at depth D4 only where learning attaches to a failure trigger.
numbers: 10 architectures, 8 runtime families, 42 systems; evidence coded E1-E4, depth D0-D4. Soar chunking to Reflexion/AgentHER rated E3/D4.
limits: Coding is by the authors, not a measured result. Little Soar episodic or semantic detail.
agent_relevance: Residual gap named: typed impasse with isolated substate and compiled resolution. Matches our S6 design.

source: Gorski, Laird (2011) Learning to use episodic memory (Cognitive Systems Research)
url: not opened; cited in Wallace et al. 2013
finding: Cited as the Soar work on learning when and how to use episodic retrieval. Not read.
numbers: Not read; no numbers.
limits: Unopened.
agent_relevance: Candidate source for the next pass.

source: Nason, Laird (2005) Soar-RL: Integrating reinforcement learning with Soar
url: not opened; cited in Laird 2022 and CoALA
finding: Original Soar-RL paper. Not read; only the later review description is used.
numbers: Not read; no numbers.

source: Derbinsky, Laird (2009) Efficiently implementing episodic memory (ICCBR)
finding: Search snippet says storage and retrieval was efficient enough for real time, about 50 ms typical match, with 1M episodes over 14 hours. Not read.
numbers: 1M episodes, 14 h, 50 ms (snippet only).
limits: Unopened; secondary snippet.
